title: The Bench
part: PART THREE: THE HIGH AND THE HOLE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #37: Sit on the bench and count everyone else's mistakes but your own.*

The new video is worse than the first. It has a title card that says "Mud Hens Meltdown," followed by a slow-motion replay of me screaming at Priya. My face is twisted, my mouth open wide, looking like a goldfish that has been pulled from a bowl and left on a counter. It has two thousand views. That is a lot of people. That is a lot of eyes.

I am sitting on the edge of my bed. My phone is buzzing on the nightstand. It is Nia. She sent a text at 7:04 AM. It just says, "Call me?" Two words. A question mark. It is the kindest thing I have seen all week. I look at the screen, then at the ceiling, then back at the phone again. I do not call.

I pick up the phone and slide it under my pillow. The buzzing stops. The room is quiet. I grab the pillow and slide it under the bed. I sit there for a long time. The phone is hidden. The problem is not hidden. The problem is inside my head, and it is loud.
pages.image: A 12-year-old girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband sits on a bed edge, sliding a glowing phone under a pillow, looking distressed in a messy bedroom.

pages.text:
Practice starts without music or drills, just the wind rattling the chain-link fence and the sudden, heavy silence. Coach Gin stands before the whiteboard, skipping her usual speech. Instead of shouting orders, she simply writes names on the board.

Priya. Tank. Leo. Mateo. Josie. Ahmed. Ollie. Plus two substitutes.

My name is missing.

I step forward, my voice cracking. "Coach, the team needs me. I am the captain. I am the engine. We cannot run without the engine."

Coach Gin caps her marker. She looks at me with a calmness that feels like a locked door. She says, "Take a week on the bench."

"But—"

"Watch," she says. "That is the first thing I have heard you say all season that isn't true."

I stand there, my mouth open, wanting to shout and cry at the same time until my eyes sting. I walk to the bench and sit down, feeling completely empty inside.
pages.image: A silver-braided coach in a yellow jacket stands by a blank white easel board with scribbled arrows with names written on it, ignoring a furious brown-skinned girl in a red jersey who is standing in front of her.

pages.text:
From the bench, the field looks bigger, but it is also quieter, which is strange because Josie is on the wing and she never stops talking. Today, however, her voice is different. She is calling out the space before it opens. "Gap on the left! Space on the right!" It sounds like the navigation app in my dad’s bus, guiding us exactly where to go without the usual screaming. I have never once heard her be this useful.

Tank is in defense. He stops trying to chase the ball and stands tall instead, taking up space like a very polite refrigerator. He is a wall. A gentle wall, but a wall all the same. The twins have a signal. Leo taps his knee, and Mateo moves. It is invisible and it is perfect.

Priya stands very still in the goal. Her gloves are on, and she looks at nothing, then everything. She is not terrified. She is waiting.

I watch them. I watch the game. I watch myself. I am just a girl on a bench, not the captain, just a girl.
pages.image: A tiny girl with glasses and oversized gloves stands motionless in a soccer goal, while other players move dynamically around her on a muddy field.

pages.text:
Nobody yells at me, which is actually the worst part.

I am waiting for it, really hoping someone will say, "You are terrible," or maybe "You don't belong here." I am braced for the anger because I know how to fight with a weapon. Anger is a shield, and I know how to hold it up.

But no one does it.

Ahmed is warming up beside me, stretching his hamstrings with the serious focus of a kid doing homework. He is quiet. He is definitely not admiring his shoelaces.

"I passed four times today," he says, not looking at me.

"That's because you were good," I say, my voice sounding very small.

Ahmed looks at me, shrugs, and says, "That's because I was on a team."

He walks away. I sit on the bench, realizing I am not the engine, just one piece of the machine, and I have been acting like I am the whole thing.
pages.image: Two boys stretch on a sideline bench, one looking at the other with a thoughtful expression, while a muddy soccer field stretches out behind them.

pages.text:
I get home, skip dinner, and go straight to my room. The red notebook is waiting on my desk, open to page one. I read the first few lines until the ink starts to swim and blur into a gray, muddy mess.

*Way to Lose #1: Show up.*
*Way to Lose #2: Let the ball hit your shin.*
*Way to Lose #3: Trust the wrong person.*

I keep reading. My handwriting looks different now. It looks smaller. I see the pattern hiding in the margins. Every line is about what someone else did to me. Or what I think they did. I have been writing down their applause. Their disappointment. Their love. None of it is actually mine. It is all borrowed.

I pick up my pen. I try to write number thirty-seven. The tip hovers over the paper. It wobbles. It looks like a confused fly trying to find a spot on a window to land.

*Way to Lose #37: ...*

I stare at the blank space. I cannot finish the sentence. I do not know how to lose anymore. I do not know how to be anything else.

The door creaks open.

Luz stands in the doorway. She is holding a thick, very blue crayon. It is the kind that snaps if you breathe on it wrong.

"Deputy says try again," she says.
pages.image: A small girl with pigtails stands in a doorway holding a blue crayon, looking at a distressed older sister who is writing in a red notebook.
